title: Vascular Medical Quality and Patient Safety -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Vascular medicine is the branch of medicine specializing in the prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of arteries, veins, and lymphatics. Healthcare providers in vascular medicine have obligations to deliver quality in the care they provide to patients. Quality control management is either not a part of the curriculum for health care professionals in vascular medicine in the United States or is of a limited extent. The prevalence of vascular disease in the United States remains relatively high in men and certain ethnic groups compared to the prevalence in other countries. Data indicate that, on a collective basis, American patients receiving care for vascular diseases suffer numerous injuries and deaths due to deficiencies in health care safety. This article highlights concepts that the interprofessional team can use to provide higher quality and safer care.

content: Objectives: Describe the role of healthcare providers in why the United States lags behind other countries in vascular health care quality metrics. title: Vascular Medical Quality and Patient Safety -- Introduction
content: This topic introduces key principles of healthcare quality assurance and patient safety as they apply to vascular medicine. Vascular medicine focuses on the prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of disorders affecting the arterial, venous, and lymphatic systems and intersects with multiple specialties, including internal medicine, cardiology, hematology, vascular surgery, wound care, rehabilitation medicine, and radiology. Although vessels supplying the brain and heart are part of the vascular system, their management is typically overseen by neurologic and cardiologic specialists. It falls outside the scope of this discussion.

title: Vascular Medical Quality and Patient Safety -- Introduction
content: In the United States, the most common non-neurologic and non-cardiologic vascular conditions are peripheral arterial disease, most commonly associated with atherosclerosis, and venous thrombosis. Peripheral arterial disease remains highly prevalent, particularly among men and certain ethnic populations, with lifestyle factors playing a significant contributory role. [1] Improving the quality of vascular care at both the individual and population levels depends on identifying healthcare structures and processes that influence outcomes, reinforcing those that support optimal care, and modifying or eliminating those that impede desired results.

title: Vascular Medical Quality and Patient Safety -- Issues of Concern -- Regulation, Administration, Fragmentation of Care, and Ethical Problems in Vascular Medicine
content: Healthcare facility administrators and policymakers who impact the practice of vascular medicine often pay lip service to the notion that they promote quality. Medicare, Medicaid, and private insurers (payers) manage hospitals through cost-containment incentive payments, and HCP employers manage HCPs through productivity incentive metrics. Physicians who perform invasive procedures are incentivized to recommend them, even when they have not been shown to outperform less invasive therapies, because such procedures yield higher RVUs and translate into increased payment. Research studies confirm that cost-containment and productivity-based financial incentives lead to cost reduction and incentive-related output increases, respectively. [5] [6]  Neither type of behavior improves quality per se; on the contrary, both often result in decreased quality.

title: Vascular Medical Quality and Patient Safety -- Issues of Concern -- Regulation, Administration, Fragmentation of Care, and Ethical Problems in Vascular Medicine
content: Overtreatment, defined as offering an intervention when a patient does not meet a predictive threshold for meaningful improvement in health outcomes, is a persistent challenge in vascular medicine. Several interconnected factors, including productivity-based incentives and systemic pressures within healthcare delivery, influence vascular healthcare professionals' (VHCPs) decisions to overtreat. Misallocation of work relative value units (wRVUs) by entities responsible for assigning their value may overemphasize certain procedures while undervaluing cognitive or conservative care. Financial incentives may also favor services that provide short-term gains, despite limited evidence of superior long-term outcomes relative to lower-risk alternatives. For example, supervised exercise therapy for lower-extremity chronic arterial insufficiency can achieve outcomes comparable to invasive procedures, albeit over a longer timeframe and at lower cost and risk.

title: Vascular Medical Quality and Patient Safety -- Issues of Concern -- Regulation, Administration, Fragmentation of Care, and Ethical Problems in Vascular Medicine
content: Additional contributors include patient pressure to pursue active intervention, even in clinical scenarios where invasive treatment has not demonstrated benefit over watchful waiting. Some clinicians may also perceive intervention as a means of reducing legal liability for failure to treat. Fragmentation of care further compounds this issue, as patients with vascular disease rarely benefit from structured, multidisciplinary deliberation, such as oncology tumor boards, in which treatment options are evaluated collaboratively using evidence and clinical experience. The absence of a unified oath or an enforceable ethical framework that requires adherence to current evidence-based practices may further widen this gap. In response, Medicare began linking reimbursement to quality metrics in the early 2010s, with penalties now reaching up to a 9% reduction in payments for providers in the lowest-performing tier. Whether such quality-based incentives will ultimately outweigh volume-driven pressures in vascular medicine remains uncertain.

title: Vascular Medical Quality and Patient Safety -- Issues of Concern -- Research Problems
content: Research in vascular medicine poses several challenges. Technology, such as stent technology, changes rapidly; demonstrating the technology's efficacy on a composite basis over time is often inadequate before the technology is offered to patients at high cost, with safety and efficacy ratios that remain unknown (as in the case of inferior vena cava filters). The generalizability of research on determining treatment efficacy in vascular medicine is limited by myriad disease patterns that affect arteries and veins differently across individuals. The natural history of disease in persons who present with arterial insufficiency syndromes of the lower extremity and/or carotid distribution or with aneurysms tends to have a fairly high risk.

title: Vascular Medical Quality and Patient Safety -- Issues of Concern -- Research Problems
content: Since almost any type of treatment, conservative measures such as SET, or medical treatment for hypertension, cholesterol, and triglycerides, will improve these conditions, it is sometimes difficult to distinguish among treatments with respect to quality and safety. Although vascular medicine lends itself to RCTs, the complexity of the disease in the research process may be sacrificed in favor of the "easier" approach of simply isolating a new treatment group and a control group and measuring a difference between them.

title: Vascular Medical Quality and Patient Safety -- Issues of Concern -- Safety Problems
content: Safety in vascular medicine (as in medicine at large) in the United States became a widespread concern only after the National Academy of Medicine (then known as the Institute of Medicine) published a report for the U.S. Congress titled "To Err is Human." [7] Issues that are unique to vascular medicine can be divided into two categories: conservative (noninvasive) and interventional (invasive) management.

title: Vascular Medical Quality and Patient Safety -- Issues of Concern -- Interventional Treatment Setting
content: In the interventional treatment setting, vascular procedures carry inherent risks. Common complications include hemorrhage, thrombosis, embolism, pseudoaneurysm formation, and arteriovenous fistulas. Vascular injury may also result in downstream consequences, such as ischemia or infarction of tissues supplied or drained by the affected vessels. Multiple safety-preserving measures are employed to reduce these risks, which can be broadly categorized into communication, image guidance, and human factors engineering. Effective communication is essential, and verbal reconfirmation in a team setting should be performed with the patient to verify patient identity, the planned procedure, and the treatment site. [8] Image guidance is increasingly used to reduce procedural invasiveness; however, endovascular image-guided therapies introduce unique hazards. Fluoroscopic guidance involves ionizing radiation, which can cause tissue injury ranging from skin burns to an increased risk of malignancy. [9] These procedures may also require iodinated contrast agents, which can precipitate acute kidney injury, or carbon dioxide, which carries a risk of tissue ischemia due to air embolism. [10] Intravascular ultrasound–guided interventions offer a promising alternative to fluoroscopy by potentially reducing radiation exposure and contrast-related risks, particularly as declining technology costs may allow broader adoption in clinical practice. [11] [12]

title: Vascular Medical Quality and Patient Safety -- Issues of Concern -- Interventional Treatment Setting
content: Human factors engineering (HFE) represents an additional layer of safety by designing tasks and systems to better align with human capabilities. HFE strategies aim to reduce unnecessary motion, minimize error, and improve reliability through mistake-proof (poka-yoke) design. In vascular medicine, this approach is exemplified by the development of coaxial systems—such as sheaths, dilators, catheters, guidewires, and stopcocks—that allow seamless interoperability while preventing improper connections or exchanges.

title: Vascular Medical Quality and Patient Safety -- Issues of Concern -- Conservative Treatment Setting
content: Conservative management of vascular health includes medication, physical therapy, and dietary modification. In this setting, hemorrhages, thromboses, and other drug adverse reactions are the main complications. Patients presenting for treatment by VHCPs tend to have multiple underlying comorbid conditions, particularly hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and cardiac dysfunction. Medications for vascular conditions, such as statins, often cause side effects and affect the therapeutic window of other drugs. Although statins offer an evidence-based therapeutic advantage for reducing arterial cholesterol and inflammation and have become almost universal for treating atherosclerosis (representing one of the significant advances in clinical medicine since 1987), they frequently cause hepatotoxicity and myositis. The ACC recommends that, before starting a patient on a statin, a VHCP determine the patient's baseline alanine aminotransferase (ALT) level to detect increases attributable to the statin and guide future management decisions. [13]

title: Vascular Medical Quality and Patient Safety -- Issues of Concern -- Conservative Treatment Setting
content: The ACC stated that it does not consider there to be high-quality evidence for any particular drug side-effect monitoring algorithm. It recommended reducing the intensity of statin therapy based on patients' muscle aches or other symptoms of muscle injury severity, and that creatine kinase levels could be used as an adjunct to management. Automated alerts based on algorithms in electronic health records and medication-ordering systems can improve safety. [14] [15] The Swiss cheese theory of error occurrence suggests that safety is best achieved through a system approach rather than relying on a single healthcare provider.

title: Vascular Medical Quality and Patient Safety -- Clinical Significance -- Data Analysis From the Vascular Quality Initiative for Promotion of Quality In Vascular Medicine
content: In 2011, the SVS established its own patient safety organization, the Vascular Quality Initiative (VQI). The VQI enables its member institutions (that provide the VQI with their own data) to access the VQI's entire database, which extends to 2001 and includes data from nearly one million procedures. The VQI includes data from patients who have undergone vascular surgery or minimally invasive image-guided vascular procedures. Retrospective analyses from this database have increased exponentially since the first publication in 2014, reaching several hundred per year as of 2021. Nearly all analyses include nonrandomized data, which is poor at supporting causal inferences and does not enable accurate effect estimates. [16] Studies reporting 'important' positive associations between independent and dependent variables, using nonrandomized data, are often invalidated when subsequent randomized trials are conducted.

title: Vascular Medical Quality and Patient Safety -- Clinical Significance -- Medical Management of Patients Undergoing Surgical/Endovascular Procedures
content: Optimizing medical therapy before and after surgical or endovascular interventions is critical to improving patient outcomes. Evidence from retrospective cohort studies suggests that patients prescribed aspirin in combination with a second antiplatelet agent following revascularization for severe lower-extremity ischemia demonstrate higher survival rates at hospital discharge compared with those receiving single antiplatelet therapy alone. [18] These findings highlight the potential benefit of dual antiplatelet therapy and underscore the need for randomized controlled trials to determine whether this survival advantage persists after controlling for confounding variables.

title: Vascular Medical Quality and Patient Safety -- Clinical Significance -- Medical Management of Patients Undergoing Surgical/Endovascular Procedures
content: Similarly, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers have been independently associated with improved overall survival and amputation-free survival in patients undergoing peripheral vascular intervention for chronic limb-threatening ischemia. [19] While these observations support the routine consideration of ACEIs and ARBs in appropriate patients, randomized controlled trials are needed to confirm causality and define optimal treatment strategies.

title: Vascular Medical Quality and Patient Safety -- Clinical Significance -- Medical Management of Patients Undergoing Surgical/Endovascular Procedures
content: Oxygen-carrying capacity is another important consideration in the perioperative setting. Case-control data indicate that patients undergoing abdominal aortic aneurysm repair with low preoperative hemoglobin levels are at increased risk for postoperative acute kidney injury, and those who develop AKI have reduced survival compared with patients without this complication. [20] These findings suggest that vascular healthcare professionals should establish consensus-based hemoglobin thresholds to optimize oxygen delivery before AAA repair and potentially reduce perioperative morbidity and mortality.

title: Vascular Medical Quality and Patient Safety -- Clinical Significance -- Patient Risk Stratification
content: Accurate risk stratification is essential for selecting appropriate candidates for vascular interventions and for counseling patients regarding expected outcomes. Overall disease burden and functional status are important predictors of prognosis. In patients undergoing endovascular abdominal aortic aneurysm repair, those with low Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) functional status scores experienced higher inpatient mortality and increased one-year post-procedure mortality compared with patients who had normal ECOG scores. [21] These findings suggest that ECOG performance status is a useful predictor of mortality risk in this clinical setting.

title: Vascular Medical Quality and Patient Safety -- Clinical Significance -- Patient Risk Stratification
content: Baseline anatomic characteristics also influence procedural success. Case-control data demonstrate that superficial femoral arteries with smaller native calibers are less likely to maintain patency following angioplasty alone when compared with larger-caliber vessels. [22]  This observation indicates that patients with small-diameter SFAs carry a higher risk of poor angioplasty outcomes and may require alternative or adjunctive treatment strategies.

[22]  This observation indicates that patients with small-diameter SFAs carry a higher risk of poor angioplasty outcomes and may require alternative or adjunctive treatment strategies.

title: Vascular Medical Quality and Patient Safety -- Clinical Significance -- Hospital Resource Meaningful Use
content: Efficient utilization of hospital resources is critical for optimizing patient outcomes while minimizing unnecessary costs. Postoperative care following abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) repair illustrates this principle. Retrospective cohort data indicate that hospitals that implemented blanket intensive care unit admission for all post-AAA repair patients had longer lengths of stay without improvements in morbidity or mortality compared with institutions that selectively admitted patients based on postoperative health status. [23] These findings suggest that routine admission to the intensive care unit for all patients does not represent meaningful use of hospital resources.

title: Vascular Medical Quality and Patient Safety -- Clinical Significance -- Hospital Resource Meaningful Use
content: Similar considerations apply to diagnostic and anesthetic services. Preoperative stress testing in patients undergoing AAA repair did not significantly reduce perioperative cardiac events or mortality compared with patients who did not receive testing. [24] [25] This suggests that routine stress testing may not constitute a meaningful use of resources. Likewise, patients undergoing outpatient brachiocephalic fistula creation under general anesthesia experienced higher hospital admissions and similar one-year access patency and reintervention rates compared with patients receiving regional anesthesia. [26] These data support regional anesthesia as a safer and more resource-efficient option for many procedures not involving open chest, abdominal, or pelvic repairs.

title: Vascular Medical Quality and Patient Safety -- Clinical Significance -- Health Law Creation and Enforcement
content: Health policy and legislation significantly influence patient access to care and procedural outcomes. Evidence demonstrates that patients with aortic aneurysms residing in states that implemented Medicaid expansion under federal guidelines underwent higher rates of elective repair and experienced fewer procedural complications compared with patients in non-expansion states. [27] These findings suggest that access to health insurance allows patients to receive timely interventions before conditions reach high-risk stages.

title: Vascular Medical Quality and Patient Safety -- Clinical Significance -- Health Law Creation and Enforcement
content: Similarly, patients with kidney failure in Medicaid expansion states were more likely to receive definitive surgical treatment according to National Kidney Foundation guidelines, bypassing temporizing non-surgical pre-dialysis care, with Hispanic patients experiencing particularly notable benefits. [28] This indicates that insurance coverage supports access to interventions that yield long-term clinical benefit, rather than to emergency measures with less favorable outcomes. Public health policies, such as tobacco taxation, have also been associated with reduced cigarette use among patients with intermittent claudication, highlighting the role of financial incentives in modifying high-risk behaviors in vascular disease populations. [29]

title: Vascular Medical Quality and Patient Safety -- Clinical Significance -- Cost of Care and Its Ramifications for Decisions on Care Reimbursement or Recommendations
content: A comparison of Medicare claims paid between patients undergoing elective endovascular or open AAA repair between 2004 and 2015 found no long-term differences in cumulative disease-related costs. The findings suggest that recommendations and policies for endovascular vs. surgical treatment for these patients should not be based on the relative costs of these procedures at particular institutions. [30]

title: Vascular Medical Quality and Patient Safety -- Clinical Significance -- Federal and Other National Healthcare Organization Guidelines/Standards
content: Guidelines and standards from federal and national healthcare organizations play a critical role in patient screening, treatment selection, and quality measurement. For abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) detection, Society for Vascular Surgery (SVS) criteria have been shown to identify patients at higher risk of AAA development more effectively than U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) criteria. [31] This finding suggests that task forces developing national recommendations for vascular medicine may benefit from including vascular specialists alongside general physicians.

title: Vascular Medical Quality and Patient Safety -- Clinical Significance -- Federal and Other National Healthcare Organization Guidelines/Standards
content: Regarding patient selection for invasive therapy, SVS guidelines recommend achieving at least two years of symptom-free recurrence in 50% of outpatients undergoing interventions for intermittent claudication. However, data indicate that only about one-third of patients achieve this benchmark regardless of whether endovascular or surgical techniques are used. [32] This highlights that the national standard may not reflect realistic clinical outcomes. Quality measurement metrics also vary: review of 154 AAA repair patients found that the American College of Surgeons’ NSQIP and the SVS Vascular Quality Initiative (VQI) databases detected clinically relevant complications more effectively than the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) patient safety indicators (PSIs), suggesting that AHRQ PSIs may not be optimal for grading hospital performance in AAA repair. [33] Finally, in monitoring radiation exposure during procedures, dose area product provides a more accurate measure than fluoroscopy time when compared with calculated air kerma, indicating that tracking dose area product is preferable when available. [34]

title: Vascular Medical Quality and Patient Safety -- Clinical Significance -- Local Hospital Policy on Postoperative Patient Follow-up
content: Patients who were lost to follow-up after endovascular AAA repair had worse outcomes than patients who remained in clinical surveillance after the procedure. [35] This suggests that VHCPs and healthcare administrators should maintain communication with patients even after they have undergone "definitive" invasive treatments for AAAs.

title: Vascular Medical Quality and Patient Safety -- Clinical Significance -- Procedure Time Planning
content: Individual patient characteristics, specific surgical maneuvers, and types of complications were quantified by the additional time they added to procedures. [36] This suggests that managers should adjust planned procedure times in light of these factors.

title: Vascular Medical Quality and Patient Safety -- Clinical Significance -- Physician Assessment
content: The number of years of experience performing a particular surgery (below-the-knee arterial reconstruction) was more closely associated with achieving a low number of surgical complications than the volume of those surgeries the surgeon performed in the last year. [37]  This suggests that more experienced surgeons who are doing fewer procedures can still perform as well as surgeons of any age performing more procedures, and that reaching a 'magic number' on a case log for the number of procedures performed in a defined recent period is not the best predictor of procedural competency, contrary to what some hospital credentialing officials may believe.

title: Vascular Medical Quality and Patient Safety -- Clinical Significance -- Patient-Customer Experience
content: Patients with varicose veins who chose telemedicine evaluations before decisions for next steps in invasive venous therapy had equivalent outcomes to patients with similar preoperative demographics and disease severity who chose traditional in-person evaluations (which require greater time and cost for the patient). [38]  This implies that the patient-customer experience can be improved by offering telemedicine evaluations for these patients.

title: Vascular Medical Quality and Patient Safety -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Teamwork can improve the quality of care in vascular medicine. [39] [40]  The cited studies describe how a team of vascular healthcare providers working together reduced minor errors, major errors, and the unnecessary exposure of patients to risks during aneurysm repair procedures. The beneficial effects of collaboration and effective communication among healthcare team members are discussed elsewhere by the authors, as well as specifically in the context of vascular medicine by other authors. [41] [42] The synchrony between quality and compensation will increase in the future, but has not yet been significant in vascular medicine. Healthcare providers and administrators should be aware of areas within vascular medicine where improvements in patient care quality are warranted. They should make data-driven decisions, guided by evidence-based guidelines from appropriate national or international organizations, to modify processes and structures that improve clinical outcomes and patient experiences while reducing costs. Cost containment and revenue generation should not compromise patient safety.
